props.title: The Great Buck Howard

sections.content: The Great Buck Howard (2008) sits at a fascinating intersection of showbiz nostalgia and mentor-mentee dynamics, following John Malkovich's pitch-perfect portrayal of a fading mentalist based on real-life performer The Amazing Kreskin. Like My Favorite Year (1982) and Me and Orson Welles (2009), it captures the bittersweet experience of a young person working alongside an aging entertainment icon. The film particularly excels in depicting the dying art of vaudeville-style performance, reminiscent of the way Ed Wood (1994) celebrated old Hollywood's fringes.

sections.content: What sets The Great Buck Howard apart is its exploration of fame's twilight years, showing a performer who peaked decades ago but maintains unwavering conviction in his relevance. This theme resonates with films like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962), though Howard takes a gentler, more affectionate approach. The father-son dynamic between real-life father and son Tom and Colin Hanks adds another layer of authenticity to the story of generational disconnect and understanding.

The film's portrayal of small-town entertainment and the grinding reality of the touring circuit recalls Paper Moon (1973) and State and Main (2000), showing how show business operates outside the glamorous spotlight. Malkovich's performance captures both the grandeur and pathos of a performer who refuses to acknowledge his diminished status, creating a character both frustrating and endearing. sections.content: The film's depiction of mentalism and stage magic connects to a rich tradition of movies about performers and illusionists. While films like Now You See Me (2013) and The Illusionist (2006) treat magic as spectacle, The Great Buck Howard focuses on the human element behind the tricks, similar to the approach taken in Deceptive Practice: The Mysteries and Mentors of Ricky Jay (2012).
